Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Below are his thoughts on the new variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Image, and more features added to the iPhone 18 Pro.

Stalman takes a deep dive into the variable aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro camera.

Although this year's iPhone 18 Pro brings a number of new features, including the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapour chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, there's no question that the biggest camera upgrade is the all-new variable aperture system.

Other new features this year include updates to Cinematic mode, new texture controls added to Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Image, and further refinements to the pro controls in the Camera app.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman published a review taking a detailed look at all the new hardware and software features of the iPhone 18 Pro, joining a flood of reviews that have appeared since the review embargo lifted — including our own.

Stalman notes that while he loves last year's Cosmic Orange colour on the iPhone 17 Pro, that colour can show up in reflections when shooting through glass. For that reason, he says, pro photographers may want to go with burgundy or black, as those colours are less likely to cast unwanted hues into your photos or videos.

He also makes it clear upfront that this review compares the iPhone 18 Pro camera to the iPhone 15 Pro, and that the review video itself was shot almost entirely on the iPhone 17 Pro.

Speaking of the biggest main camera upgrade this year — the new variable aperture — Stalman calls the change "a step toward making the iPhone a truly professional camera."

He also notes that the larger f/1.48 aperture lets more light reach the sensor, helping to keep ISO lower in low-light situations and reducing reliance on Night mode.

This portion of the review showcases some great shots of the aperture blades opening and closing. Stalman points out that Apple's design is rather unique — the aperture blades are placed in front of the main lens element, rather than sitting deeper inside the lens stack like on traditional camera lenses.

Stalman also mentions that the 4x zoom on the iPhone 18 Pro (which was also present last year's model) is a noticeable improvement over the 5x zoom on the iPhone 16 Pro, which could sometimes feel a bit too tight.

Speaking of which, he also touches on the new AI editing tools, such as Clean Up, Extend, and Reframe. He says while these tools are technically impressive and produce very convincing results, they can make significant alterations to an image, leaving the result feeling quite different from the original photo.

Moving on to the new texture options on the iPhone 18 Pro, including Soft Skin, Glow, and Film, Stalman walks through the intensity of each effect from 0 to 100. His take: Soft Skin can subtly reduce skin detail rather than simply blurring the skin, while Glow acts like a black mist filter to create soft highlights.

He is also impressed by the grain and blooming of the Film effect, though he wishes Apple would give users more control over the amount of grain.

The review also touches on Apple Reference Image, Cinematic mode on the iPhone (Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic results), and the new Apple Log 2. The video naturally also includes plenty of photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.
